prompt.context_jp: 副チーフの音羽の前には、蜂毒でショック状態に陥ったレスキュー隊員___横たわり、看護師ミンの手が休むことなく動いていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: レスキュー隊員___横たわり
prompt.prompt_en: The rescue team member is being introduced as a new element on the scene. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: The rescue member is newly presented to the reader — Otowa walks up and we see him there for the first time. New-information subjects of descriptive 'there is/lay' sentences take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make him the already-known topic, as if we had been discussing him; but the sentence is literally introducing him to the scene.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋には男が座っていた。
contrast_examples.en: There was a man sitting in the room. (new info → が)

contrast_examples.jp: その男は窓の方を見ていた。
contrast_examples.en: The man was looking toward the window. (now a known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 危険を顧みずに飛び出したミンの背中を、彼___追いきれず、胸の奥にわずかな苛立ちを残したままだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼___追いきれず
prompt.prompt_en: The focus shifts back to Otowa, the established viewpoint character. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: 彼 (Otowa) is the already-established topic — we've been inside his head. は marks him as the known theme whose state the sentence describes.
feedback.incorrect_en: が here would read as singling him out as new/contrastive information, which clashes with the fact that we've been following him all along.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は追いつけなかった。
contrast_examples.en: He couldn't catch up. (known topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 追いついたのは彼が最初だった。
contrast_examples.en: He was the first to catch up. (identifying who → が)

prompt.context_jp: ミンの上腕には、赤く腫れあがった刺し傷___残っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 刺し傷___残っていた
prompt.prompt_en: A wound is being revealed on Min's arm. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: The sting mark is being introduced — Otowa (and the reader) notice it for the first time. Existence/discovery sentences take が on the newly presented noun.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose the wound as already known and contrast it with something else, which doesn't match this moment of discovery.

contrast_examples.jp: 机の上に本がある。
contrast_examples.en: There is a book on the desk. (new info → が)

contrast_examples.jp: その本は面白い。
contrast_examples.en: That book is interesting. (known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: それを確かめる音羽の指先___、ふだんよりもいくぶん慎重だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 音羽の指先___、ふだんよりもいくぶん慎重だった
prompt.prompt_en: The sentence contrasts today's gentleness with his usual manner. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: The implicit contrast is 'today vs. usual' — a classic contrastive は use. It frames his fingertips as the theme and sets up the comparison with ふだんより.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would simply present his fingertips as new information, losing the contrastive 'more cautious than usual' nuance that the sentence builds.

contrast_examples.jp: 今日は彼の声は優しかった。
contrast_examples.en: Today his voice was gentle. (implied contrast with other days)

contrast_examples.jp: 急に彼の声が震えた。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly his voice trembled. (new event → が)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見の表情___わずかに硬くなった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 喜多見の表情___わずかに硬くなった
prompt.prompt_en: A sudden change in Kitami's face is being reported as a new event. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: This is a sudden, observable change — a classic event report. が presents the new occurrence (his expression stiffening) rather than commenting on an established topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn it into a general comment on his expression as a known theme, losing the 'just now, suddenly' feeling of the moment.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の顔が青ざめた。
contrast_examples.en: His face turned pale. (sudden change → が)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の顔はいつも穏やかだ。
contrast_examples.en: His face is always calm. (general statement → は)

prompt.context_jp: 手にした児童名簿を、彼___指先で追いはじめる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼___指先で追いはじめる
prompt.prompt_en: Kitami is the ongoing subject in this scene. Pick the particle for 彼.

feedback.correct_en: Kitami is the established viewpoint — we were just reading about his expression stiffening. は keeps him as the topic whose next action we're following.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would single him out as new/exhaustive ('it is HE who starts tracing'), but no one else is being contrasted here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は名簿をめくり始めた。
contrast_examples.en: He began flipping through the roster. (topic continuation)

contrast_examples.jp: めくったのは彼が最初だった。
contrast_examples.en: He was the first to flip through it. (identifying → が)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見の視線___ふと横に立つ冬木へと向けられた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 喜多見の視線___ふと横に向けられた
prompt.prompt_en: A sudden movement of gaze is reported. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: ふと ('suddenly') signals an event unfolding before our eyes. が is used for such momentary-change reports where the subject is spotlighted as new information.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 視線 as a known topic ('as for his gaze, …'), weakening the sudden-event feel that ふと sets up.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の目がきらりと光った。
contrast_examples.en: His eyes suddenly flashed. (event → が)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の目はいつも鋭い。
contrast_examples.en: His eyes are always sharp. (general → は)

prompt.context_jp: 冬木の顔から___血の気が引いていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冬木の顔から___血の気が引いていた
prompt.prompt_en: The phrase 'from his face' is being singled out as the specific site where color drained. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: Attaching は to から emphasizes the face specifically — 'from his face in particular (not elsewhere), the color drained.' It foregrounds the location as a thematic contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: が cannot attach after から in this role; the sentence already uses が on 血の気 as the subject. からは is the natural way to spotlight the source.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔からは汗が噴き出していた。
contrast_examples.en: Sweat was pouring from his face (specifically).

contrast_examples.jp: 顔から汗が流れた。
contrast_examples.en: Sweat ran from his face. (neutral)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見___その横顔に、いつもの穏やかな麻酔科医とは違うものを見て取った。
prompt.prompt_jp: 喜多見___その横顔に…違うものを見て取った
prompt.prompt_en: Kitami is the known observer here. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: Kitami is the established viewpoint character leading this scene. は marks him as the topic whose perception the sentence describes.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would imply 'it was Kitami (not someone else) who noticed,' but no exhaustive/identificational contrast is being made here.

contrast_examples.jp: 喜多見はその変化に気づいた。
contrast_examples.en: Kitami noticed the change. (topic)

contrast_examples.jp: そのとき誰かが気づいた。喜多見が、だ。
contrast_examples.en: Someone noticed then — it was Kitami. (identifying → が)

prompt.context_jp: 冬木の唇___震え、それ以上の言葉が続かない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冬木の唇___震え
prompt.prompt_en: A sudden involuntary bodily reaction is being reported. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: Body-part reactions reported as an unfolding event ('his lips trembled') take が. The focus is on the physical change happening before us.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 唇 a thematic topic ('as for his lips…'), which sounds oddly analytic for a sudden emotional reaction.

contrast_examples.jp: 手が震えた。
contrast_examples.en: His hands trembled. (event → が)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の手はいつも温かい。
contrast_examples.en: His hands are always warm. (general property → は)

prompt.context_jp: 冬木の顔___青ざめ、彼は矢も盾もたまらず走り出そうとした。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冬木の顔___青ざめ
prompt.prompt_en: Another sudden change on Fuyuki's face. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: The face turning pale is a sudden, observable event triggered by the shocking news. が reports this change as it happens.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would thematize 'his face' as if comparing it to something else, which doesn't fit this reactive, in-the-moment description.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔が真っ赤になった。
contrast_examples.en: His face turned bright red. (event → が)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の顔は赤かった。
contrast_examples.en: His face was red. (describing a known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 冬木の膝___崩れ、その名を呼ぶ声が喉の奥で痙攣した。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冬木の膝___崩れ
prompt.prompt_en: His knees give way at the sight of his son. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: An uncontrollable, momentary bodily event — knees buckling — is naturally reported with が. The focus is on the thing happening to his body right now.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would introduce a contrast or general comment about his knees, which is out of place in this urgent moment of collapse.

contrast_examples.jp: 足が止まった。
contrast_examples.en: His feet stopped (involuntarily). (event → が)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の足は速い。
contrast_examples.en: He is fast on his feet. (general trait → は)

prompt.context_jp: 冬木___言葉をこらえきれず、息子の額にそっと自分の額を寄せた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冬木___言葉をこらえきれず、…寄せた
prompt.prompt_en: Fuyuki is the ongoing focus character. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: Fuyuki is the established protagonist of this emotional scene — we've been watching his reactions. は marks him as the topic whose action is described.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would suggest identifying/singling him out from others, but the narration is simply continuing with him as the known subject.

contrast_examples.jp: 冬木は息子を抱きしめた。
contrast_examples.en: Fuyuki hugged his son. (topic continuation)

contrast_examples.jp: 最初に動いたのは冬木が、だった。
contrast_examples.en: The one who moved first was Fuyuki. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見の顔から、いつもの余裕___すでに消えていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: いつもの余裕___すでに消えていた
prompt.prompt_en: The sentence contrasts his 'usual composure' against this moment. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: いつもの余裕 ('his usual composure') is already a known characteristic being contrasted with the present. は picks it out as the theme and sets up the contrast with the exceptional moment.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present his composure as a fresh piece of information, missing the 'the usual thing that is normally there — gone' framing.

contrast_examples.jp: いつもの笑顔は消えていた。
contrast_examples.en: His usual smile was gone. (contrast with normal)

contrast_examples.jp: 笑顔が浮かんだ。
contrast_examples.en: A smile appeared. (new, neutral event)

prompt.context_jp: 包帯の巻かれた腕を庇いながらも、その目には迷い___なかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: その目には迷い___なかった
prompt.prompt_en: In an existence/absence statement ('there was no hesitation'), which particle fits 迷い?

feedback.correct_en: With ある/ない (existence), the item whose presence or absence is being asserted takes が. The location その目に is already marked with は for contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: Using は on 迷い would double up the topic markers awkwardly and change the meaning to 'as for hesitation (in contrast with something else), there wasn't any.'

contrast_examples.jp: 顔には不安がなかった。
contrast_examples.en: There was no anxiety in his face.

contrast_examples.jp: 不安はもう消えていた。
contrast_examples.en: The anxiety had already vanished. (known topic contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 時計の針___長く延び、額の汗を看護師が丁寧に拭いとった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 時計の針___長く延び
prompt.prompt_en: A new descriptive observation about the setting during surgery. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: This is a scene-painting observation presenting the clock hands as new information in the operating room. Narrative descriptive subjects of events take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn the clock hands into a known topic being commented on, which is strange since they haven't been mentioned before in this scene.

contrast_examples.jp: 時間が過ぎていった。
contrast_examples.en: Time passed. (event description → が)

contrast_examples.jp: 時間はもう遅かった。
contrast_examples.en: It was already late. (comment on known time → は)

prompt.context_jp: モニターに映る隊員たちの姿を、彼___苦い顔で見つめていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼___苦い顔で見つめていた
prompt.prompt_en: Shirakane has just been introduced in the previous sentence as the one standing beside Akatsuka. Pick the particle for 彼.

feedback.correct_en: Shirakane has just become the established referent — は carries him forward as the ongoing topic whose action we observe.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would suggest exhaustive identification ('it was HE who was staring'), but no contrast with other watchers is in play.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は黙って見ていた。
contrast_examples.en: He watched in silence. (topic continuation)

contrast_examples.jp: 黙って見ていたのは彼だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one watching in silence was him. (identifying → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「なんで ___ をしたんです？」
prompt.prompt_jp: なんで ___ をしたんです？
prompt.prompt_en: Otowa confronts Min about dashing into danger. Which word fits?

feedback.correct_en: ムチャをする means 'to do something reckless/unreasonable.' Otowa is criticizing Min for charging in without regard for her own safety.
feedback.incorrect_en: ムダ ('waste') and ミス ('mistake') don't collocate with をする in this scolding sense — Min's action was dangerous, not wasteful or erroneous.

contrast_examples.jp: 無茶をするな。
contrast_examples.en: Don't do anything reckless.

contrast_examples.jp: 無駄なことはやめよう。
contrast_examples.en: Let's stop wasting effort.

prompt.context_jp: ミンさんの無謀な行動で 一命を ___ ました。
prompt.prompt_jp: 一命を ___ ました
prompt.prompt_en: Thanks to Min's reckless action, the rescue worker's life was saved. Pick the verb.

feedback.correct_en: 一命を取り留める is the set phrase for 'to narrowly survive / have one's life saved.' It's used especially in medical/news contexts.
feedback.incorrect_en: 受け止める means 'catch/accept,' and 引き止める means 'hold back/dissuade' — neither forms the fixed collocation with 一命.

contrast_examples.jp: 手術で一命を取り留めた。
contrast_examples.en: His life was saved by the surgery.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼を引き止めた。
contrast_examples.en: She held him back from leaving.

prompt.context_jp: 副チーフなんだと 思わず ___ ちゃいました お恥ずかしい話です
prompt.prompt_jp: 思わず ___ ちゃいました
prompt.prompt_en: Fuyuki admits he lied to his son to look impressive. Which expression fits?

feedback.correct_en: 格好をつける / 格好つける means 'to show off / try to look cool.' Fuyuki is sheepishly confessing he puffed himself up in front of his son.
feedback.incorrect_en: 気を使う ('be considerate') and 張り切る ('be energetic') don't match the embarrassed 'I was showing off' tone of his confession.

contrast_examples.jp: つい格好つけてしまった。
contrast_examples.en: I ended up showing off.

contrast_examples.jp: 張り切って準備した。
contrast_examples.en: I prepared with enthusiasm.

prompt.context_jp: 冬木の顔が青ざめ、彼は矢も盾も ___ 走り出そうとした。
prompt.prompt_jp: 矢も盾も ___ 走り出そうとした
prompt.prompt_en: Fuyuki can't bear to wait and tries to dash off. Pick the idiom.

feedback.correct_en: 矢も盾もたまらず is a set idiom meaning 'unable to bear it any longer / with uncontrollable urgency.' It perfectly captures a father desperate to reach his son.
feedback.incorrect_en: The idiom is fixed as たまらず. Substituting とまらず or かまわず breaks the phrase and produces non-standard Japanese.

contrast_examples.jp: 矢も盾もたまらず駆け出した。
contrast_examples.en: He bolted out, unable to bear it.

contrast_examples.jp: 人目もかまわず泣いた。
contrast_examples.en: He cried without caring who was watching. (different idiom)

prompt.context_jp: 彼はこみ上げる思いを ___ きれずにいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: こみ上げる思いを ___ きれずにいた
prompt.prompt_en: After surgery, Fuyuki can't fully hold back his emotions. Pick the verb.

feedback.correct_en: 抑えきれない collocates naturally with 思い/感情 to mean 'unable to hold back (one's feelings).' It's the standard phrasing for welling-up emotions.
feedback.incorrect_en: 伝えきれず ('unable to fully convey') shifts the meaning to communication, and 受けきれず doesn't collocate with こみ上げる思い here.

contrast_examples.jp: 涙を抑えきれなかった。
contrast_examples.en: I couldn't hold back my tears.

contrast_examples.jp: 気持ちを伝えきれなかった。
contrast_examples.en: I couldn't fully convey my feelings.

prompt.context_jp: すいません 彼らの力量を ___ ていました 強いですね
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼らの力量を ___ ていました
prompt.prompt_en: Shirakane admits he misjudged MER's abilities. Pick the verb.

feedback.correct_en: 見誤る means 'to misjudge / assess incorrectly.' Shirakane is confessing he underestimated the team's capabilities.
feedback.incorrect_en: 見送る ('see off / postpone') and 見逃す ('overlook / let slip') don't convey 'misjudged their ability.' 力量を見誤る is the standard collocation.

contrast_examples.jp: 相手の実力を見誤った。
contrast_examples.en: I misjudged my opponent's strength.

contrast_examples.jp: チャンスを見逃した。
contrast_examples.en: I missed the chance.

prompt.context_jp: 紛争地域で 何度も ___ においがします 恐らく 爆弾です
prompt.prompt_jp: 何度も ___ においがします
prompt.prompt_en: Komaba recognizes the smell from war zones. Which verb goes with におい?

feedback.correct_en: においを嗅ぐ ('to smell / sniff') is the standard collocation. Komaba is saying he has smelled this particular odor many times before, in conflict zones.
feedback.incorrect_en: 吸う ('inhale') suggests breathing in air, not identifying a smell; 感じた works for a vague 'sense' but においを嗅ぐ is the natural idiom for recognizing a scent.

contrast_examples.jp: 変なにおいを嗅いだ。
contrast_examples.en: I smelled a strange odor.

contrast_examples.jp: 深く息を吸った。
contrast_examples.en: He breathed in deeply.

prompt.context_jp: オペ室の患者さんを ___ のは 麻酔科医の仕事です
prompt.prompt_jp: 患者さんを ___ のは 麻酔科医の仕事です
prompt.prompt_en: Fuyuki declares the anesthesiologist's duty. Pick the verb.

feedback.correct_en: 守る ('to protect / watch over') is the key verb Fuyuki uses to redefine his role. Anesthesiologists guard patients' vitals throughout the surgery.
feedback.incorrect_en: 助ける ('rescue') fits the surgeon's cutting work, and 見る ('look at') is too weak — Fuyuki is claiming the active role of protector.

contrast_examples.jp: 患者を守るのが私の仕事です。
contrast_examples.en: My job is to protect the patient.

contrast_examples.jp: 患者を助けるために手術する。
contrast_examples.en: We operate to save the patient.

prompt.context_jp: 音羽がミンの無茶な行動を責める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: ミンの謝罪として自然なのはどちら？
prompt.prompt_en: Min apologizes for her reckless action. Which reply sounds more natural in this moment?

choices.text: すみません 夢中になって
すみません 夢中にします

feedback.correct_en: 夢中になって (te-form of 夢中になる) trails off naturally, implying '…because I got caught up in the moment.' It's the idiomatic way to explain a lapse.
feedback.incorrect_en: 夢中にします is ungrammatical in this intransitive sense. 夢中になる is the fixed phrase for 'to become absorbed/engrossed.'

contrast_examples.jp: つい夢中になってしまって。
contrast_examples.en: I just got caught up in it, sorry.

contrast_examples.jp: 子どもがゲームに夢中になる。
contrast_examples.en: The child gets absorbed in the game.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が取り乱す冬木を落ち着かせる場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 励ましの言葉として自然な語順はどちら？
prompt.prompt_en: Kitami wants to tell Fuyuki he knows his son best. Which word order sounds most natural?

choices.text: 息子さんのことは 誰よりも 冬木先生が 一番 よく分かってるはずです
冬木先生が 息子さんのことは 一番 誰よりも よく分かってるはずです

feedback.correct_en: Starting with the topic (息子さんのことは) and then stacking 誰よりも + 冬木先生が + 一番 builds emphasis cleanly — the structure Kitami actually uses to calm Fuyuki down.
feedback.incorrect_en: B scrambles the topic in the middle and places 一番 and 誰よりも awkwardly, producing a disjointed rhythm no native speaker would use in urgent speech.

contrast_examples.jp: あの件は、誰よりも彼が一番よく知っている。
contrast_examples.en: He knows about that matter better than anyone.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼があの件は一番誰よりも知っている。
contrast_examples.en: (unnatural scrambled order)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が「誰にでもできることはある」と信念を語る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 音羽の信念を伝える自然な言い方はどちら？
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds more natural for Otowa's belief?

choices.text: 誰にだって できることはあると 思いますけど
誰にだって できる事情はあると 思いますけど

feedback.correct_en: できることがある ('there is something one can do') is the natural idiomatic phrase. Otowa is pushing back on the idea that only Kitami matters — everyone has a contribution to make.
feedback.incorrect_en: 事情 means 'circumstances,' which doesn't collocate with 誰にだってできる… and changes the meaning entirely. The intended noun is こと.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰にでもできることがある。
contrast_examples.en: Everyone has something they can do.

contrast_examples.jp: それぞれの事情がある。
contrast_examples.en: Each person has their own circumstances. (different meaning)

prompt.context_jp: 冬木が助かった息子に語りかける場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 父親の言葉として自然なのはどちら？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as a father's praise?

choices.text: ああ 壮太は… パパの自慢のヒーローだ
ああ 壮太は… パパの自慢をするヒーローだ

feedback.correct_en: 自慢の + noun ('one's prized/beloved X') is a fixed, warm expression — '[my] pride-and-joy hero.' It captures the father's emotion perfectly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 自慢をするヒーロー would mean 'a hero who brags,' which inverts the meaning and makes Sota the one bragging, not the one being proud of.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は自慢の息子だ。
contrast_examples.en: He is my pride and joy of a son.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼はいつも自慢をする。
contrast_examples.en: He is always bragging. (different meaning)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が手術後に冬木の働きを称える場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: チーフが同僚に感謝を伝える自然な言い方はどちら？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as Kitami's praise after surgery?

choices.text: 冬木先生が…気を配ってくれるから 俺たちは 目の前のオペに 集中できるんです
冬木先生が…気を配ってあげるから 俺たちは 目の前のオペに 集中できるんです

feedback.correct_en: 気を配ってくれる takes the giver's perspective toward the speaker — 'you watch over us (for our benefit).' It's warm and grateful, which matches Kitami's intent.
feedback.incorrect_en: 気を配ってあげる would mean Fuyuki is doing a favor downward to someone, and sounds condescending/odd when the speaker is the recipient. Native speakers use くれる here.

contrast_examples.jp: 手伝ってくれてありがとう。
contrast_examples.en: Thanks for helping me. (benefit comes to me)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼に手伝ってあげた。
contrast_examples.en: I helped him out. (I did him a favor)
